# A simultaneous sharp boundary potential at any interior source

This is an ordinary convex-geometric theorem, proved here for arbitrary
fiber shapes and all directions at once. Its constructive actual erosion
is proved in `candidate 4e871da0351ca07a`.
The two results remove shape and cap-direction restrictions from the
FREE-source variation argument. They do not assert compatibility of
independently eroded fibers at active anchored Minkowski contacts and
therefore do not prove OC.

## 1. Statement

Let d>=1, let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, and
let y belong to its interior. There is a finite positive continuous
function Phi on S^(d-1) times R^d, convex in its second argument, such
that, writing n_K(x) for the almost everywhere defined outward unit
normal and eta for H_(d-1) on the boundary,

    D = integral_boundaryK Phi(n_K(x),x) d eta(x) > 0,

and, simultaneously for every closed halfspace H containing y,

    integral_(boundaryK intersect H) Phi(n_K(x),x) d eta(x)
         >= Gamma_d D,                 Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.       (1)

All integrals are finite. For d=1 the boundary measure is H_0 and the
normal at each of the two endpoints is used. Neither smoothness nor
strict convexity is required. In particular, any probability-weighted
finite profile of source-containing caps has the same lower bound
against this ONE potential.

The translation x -> x-y in the proof is local ordinary-fiber notation.
No projective or affine transformation of the mixed-integer lattice or
of the other fibers is performed.

## 2. An attained projective centroid normalization

Translate y to0 and put

    Omega = {a in R^d : 1+a.x>0 for every x in K},
    T_a(x) = x/(1+a.x),
    V(a) = integral_K (1+a.x)^(-d-1) dx.

Omega is nonempty, open and convex. Since r B is contained in K for
some r>0, Omega is bounded by1/r. For a in Omega the positive fractional
linear map T_a sends each segment onto the segment with the transformed
endpoints. Its inverse on its image is T_(-a). Thus T_a K is a compact
convex body containing0 in its interior. The rank-one determinant
formula gives

    det D T_a(x) = (1+a.x)^(-d-1),                 |T_a K|=V(a).   (2)

Every central halfspace and every ray are preserved. Differentiating
under the integral on compact subsets of Omega is justified by a
common positive lower bound on the denominators. In particular,

    grad V(a) = -(d+1) integral_K x(1+a.x)^(-d-2) dx,
    D^2 V(a)[b,b] = (d+1)(d+2)
                     integral_K (b.x)^2(1+a.x)^(-d-3) dx.

The last expression is strictly positive for b!=0 since K has
nonempty interior; hence V is strictly convex.

Here is the needed attainment proof. If a_k in Omega tends to a point
a_0 of its boundary, compactness of K gives x_0 in K with1+a_0.x_0=0.
Write delta_k=1+a_k.x_0>0; then delta_k ->0. Choose a small fixed
(d-1)-dimensional disk E centered at0 in a_0-perp and contained in rB.
The cone conv(x_0,E) is contained in K. Its parameterization
x=(1-t)x_0+t z has volume element c t^(d-1) dt dH_(d-1)(z), with c>0:
x_0 is not in a_0-perp. Boundedness of a_k gives uniformly
1+a_k.x <= delta_k+C t. On delta_k<=t<=2delta_k this bounds the
integrand below by a constant times delta_k^(-d-1), while the
parameterized volume is a constant times delta_k^d. Consequently
V(a_k)>=c'/delta_k -> infinity. In d=1 use the singleton E={0} and
H_0(E)=1; the same calculation applies.

Thus any sublevel of V is compactly contained in Omega, and V attains
a unique minimum a there. At this minimum, change variables by (2):

    0=integral_K x(1+a.x)^(-d-2)dx = integral_(T_a K) z dz.

The ordinary centroid of T_a K is therefore0. This independently
repeats the relevant normalization argument of
`candidate 85d2c2a949b59b29`; it does not invoke its
unproved weighted-cap comparison or any mixed-integer theorem.

## 3. A globally defined convex potential

Let delta=min_(x in K)(1+a.x)>0. Define f on ALL of R by

    f(t)=t^(-d),                                  t>=delta,
    f(t)=delta^(-d)-d delta^(-d-1)(t-delta),        t<=delta.

These pieces have the same value and derivative at delta. Their
derivatives are nondecreasing, so f is convex and C1. It is finite
and positive on R. This tangent continuation is needed: no singular
inverse power outside the original fiber is being used as a globally
convex test.

With h_K(n)=max_(x in K) n.x, set

    Phi(n,x)=h_K(n) f(1+a.x).                              (3)

Since0 is interior, h_K is positive on the unit sphere. It is
continuous, and (3) is finite, continuous, positive, and convex in x
for every fixed n. Its boundary values use the actual support identity
h_K(n_K(x))=n_K(x).x at all regular boundary points. Convex bodies have
finite surface measure and unique normal almost everywhere, so the
boundary integrals are unambiguous and finite. They are positive
because h_K and f are bounded below by positive constants on the
compact boundary. For the original untranslated coordinates replace
h_K by h_(K-y) and x by x-y in (3).

## 4. Exact cap identity

The vector field F(x)=x/(1+a.x)^d is C1 on a neighborhood of K and has

    div F(x) = d/(1+a.x)^(d+1).                           (4)

At a regular point of the original boundary its outward flux equals
Phi(n_K(x),x). Consider a central halfspace H={u.x>=0}, u!=0.
Gauss--Green on the convex body K intersect H gives

    integral_(boundaryK intersect H) Phi d eta
          = d integral_(K intersect H)(1+a.x)^(-d-1) dx
          = d |T_a K intersect H|.                         (5)

Indeed the new planar part of the boundary has normal parallel to u
and x.u=0, so its flux is zero. The intersection of that plane with
the original boundary has H_(d-1) measure zero: the central plane
crosses the interior, and the intersection is the relative boundary
of its (d-1)-dimensional convex section. In d=1 it misses both
original endpoints, and (5) is the ordinary endpoint formula. Thus
there is no positive boundary mass silently moved between an open
and a closed cap. Gauss--Green applies to nonsmooth convex bodies,
which are bounded Lipschitz domains. Applying the same identity to
the whole K gives

    D=d |T_a K|.                                          (6)

Apply the classical sharp ordinary centroid Grünbaum theorem to the
actual centroid-zero convex body T_a K. Equations (5)--(6) prove (1)
for every through0 cap with the exact factor Gamma_d. A closed
halfspace containing0 contains its parallel through0 halfspace;
positivity of the boundary measure gives (1) for it as well. This
completes the theorem.

## 5. Scope, realization, and the unresolved mixed interface

The cited ordinary Grünbaum theorem is the standard continuous
centroid theorem. No OC assumption is used. It is applied only to a
single ordinary body, not to a projective image of the mixed family.
There is no comparison asserted between original unweighted cap
volumes and transformed ones; previous counterexamples to that
comparison do not concern (5).

For any finite weights theta_j>=0 of sum1 and any containing caps,
linearity gives integral Phi sum_j theta_j 1_(H_j) d eta>=Gamma_d D.
The same potential works before any choice of these weights or caps.
This is stronger than the earlier canonical/noncanonical free-simplex
efficiency statements, but does not by itself supply feasible coupled
fiber motions. The companion source realizes it by the actual convex
erosion {g_K+epsilon f(1+a.x)<=1}, with uniform O(epsilon^2) cap-loss
error. Strict anchored inclusions permit such erosions simultaneously;
tight ones need additional proof. For d=0 use discrete arguments, not
this boundary construction. Intrinsically lower-dimensional mixed
intersections likewise require the separately proved reduction, not
an unsupported application of a d-dimensional normal measure.
